out:
{
  "hypothesis": "Predicted that negative news content would elicit higher levels of physiological arousal and attentiveness compared to neutral or positive news content across human populations.",
  "design": "within",
  "manipulation_or_predictor": "The tone of video news stories (coded as an interval-level measure of negativity).",
  "outcome_measure": "Physiological activation measured via normalized skin-conductance levels (nSCL) and heart-rate variability (RMSSD).",
  "population_and_setting": "Laboratory participants from 17 countries (Brazil, Canada, Chile, China, Denmark, France, Ghana, India, Israel, Italy, Japan, New Zealand, Russia, Senegal, Sweden, the United Kingdom, and the United States).",
  "sample_size_total": 1156,
  "recruitment_and_incentive": "Not stated.",
  "analysis_plan": "Regression models estimating the effect of story tone on physiological measures (nSCL and RMSSD), including models with and without country-level weights.",
  "preregistered_or_confirmatory": "not stated",
  "other_methods_notes": "Participants watched 7 randomly ordered BBC World News stories while wearing sensors to capture skin conductance and blood volume pulse. Data were analyzed at the respondent-story level for heart-rate variability and at 1-second intervals for skin conductance."
}
